title: Tale of Ma'an the Son of Zaidah

full_text:
Ma'an bin Zaidah was the governor of Iraq and the northern marches, renowned throughout the caliphate for his extraordinary forbearance, mildness of temper, and princely generosity. Three cynical courtiers in Basra wagered one hundred camels that they could provoke the governor into losing his temper.

A daring desert poet accepted the challenge. He dressed in ragged goat-skins, entered Ma'an’s grand hall without greeting him with royal titles, and shouted: 'Do you remember, O Ma'an, when your shoes were made of camel-hide and you tended goats in the hills?'

The courtiers gasped at the insolence, but Ma'an smiled gently and replied: 'I remember it well, brother; it was a peaceful life, and I thank heaven for the humble beginnings that taught me gratitude.'

The poet stepped closer and recited an insulting verse: 'Now that you sit on a cushioned divan, you think yourself a prince, yet your lineage is lower than the dust!'

Ma'an answered with undisturbed calm: 'A man’s true lineage is his conduct, my friend. If my deeds are worthy, my origin matters little; and if my deeds are evil, no noble ancestry can redeem me.'

The poet, enraged by his failure to ruffle the governor, shouted: 'Give me five hundred pieces of gold at once, you miserly son of a shepherd, or I shall mock you across every market from Basra to Damascus!'

Ma'an turned to his treasurer and said with boundless courtesy: 'Give this man a thousand pieces of gold: five hundred for his bold poetry, and five hundred because his clothing is thin and the winter frost approaches.'

The poet dropped his staff, fell upon his knees before the governor, and kissed his robe: 'By the Creator of all things, O Ma'an, your forbearance is a fortress that no tongue can breach! I came to provoke your anger for a wager, but your magnanimity has conquered my soul forever.' Ma'an smiled, raised the poet to his feet, and welcomed him as a friend of his court.
moral: Patience and forbearance under insult prove true nobility more than swords and royal decrees.
